description_full: Innovative Aerosystems, Inc., engages in the engineering, manufacturing, and supply of advanced avionic solutions. The company provides autothrottles; LPV Navigators; standby displays; COM/NAV/surveillance radio management systems; air data solutions; inertial reference systems; utilities management systems; and air data, attitude and heading reference systems. It also offers flat panel display systems, inertial reference systems, integrated global navigation systems, global positioning systems, c-130 engine instrument display systems, liberty flight deck, and communications/navigation products. The company serves business aircrafts, commercial airlines, military, virtual cp-pilots, and turbo prop. The company was formerly known as Innovative Solutions and Support, Inc. and changed its name to Innovative Aerosystems, Inc. in October 2025. Innovative Aerosystems, Inc. was incorporated in 1988 and is based in Exton, Pennsylvania.
ceo_bio: Dr. Shahram  Askarpour | President, CEO & Director | Age 68 | Compensation: $1.3M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 147 people. Revenue per employee of $573K ranks in the top quartile among Industrials peers, with revenue growing 9%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $46K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $16K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Innovative Solutions and Suppor is a small-cap industrials business with a $377M market cap on $84M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +45% over the past three years and +15% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 20% against a 9% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 54% confirm genuine pricing power.
The business throws off $7M in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.85× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 11.6×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 9.8% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 24% operating margin runs 15pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.14x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+32.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 127% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 6% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 32% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 77% and a beta of 0.91, it moves roughly with the market.
About $4.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 58% in the 2020 crash, 40% in the 2022 bear market and 74% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $11.51 (margin of safety -83%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 41%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $7.28 to $18.02 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/FCF 55.5 vs 22.9 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-8%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $33.25 on average, 58% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 20% clears the cost of capital of 9.0% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.99).
It runs a 54% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 24% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 13pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 4.7% of revenue on R&D and 2.8% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.9x net debt to EBITDA ($2.7M of cash against $24.1M of debt), with interest covered 11.6x.
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation.
Working capital ties up about 241 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 44.8% over 3 years, 31.3% over 5 years and 15.4% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 33%).
At current returns, reinvesting 60% of profits supports about 11.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 26.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.90 (orders lagging sales) and a backlog worth 17% of annual revenue.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (7.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders own 9.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 62%.
The share count has grown 0.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 147 employees, each generates about $573K of revenue, 1.6x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 8.8% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $46K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.3M (2x revenue per employee).
